Monday, 5 June. After three months of maternity leave, Ioana is going back to Atelier Rhône, part-time. Her boss, Nathalie, is waiting for her with the schedule for the Fourvière site.
Ioana! We missed you. Sit down. Coffee? Oh no, sorry, you don’t drink it any more.
I’ll start again when Rose-Hélène has learned to sleep past six in the morning. So around 2035.
(laughs) Right. Let’s talk about Fourvière. The inauguration is set for 15 September. The mayor is coming, and the press too.
The 15th? That’s tight. How are the works going?
The walls and windows are finished. But the parquet is behind schedule. The supplier must have written down the wrong date, I suppose.
Then let’s make a precise schedule. As soon as the parquet has arrived, the workers will lay it. How long?
Three weeks. Then, once they’ve laid it, it will have to be left to dry before we install the stage.
So if all goes well, by the end of July we’ll have finished the main structure. And the piano?
It will be delivered once the room has been cleaned. End of August. Will you have time to breathe in July, with your daughter?
She starts at the nursery next week. Once she’s got used to it, I’ll be able to work in the afternoons too.
Perfect. And in August you’re going to Romania for the christening, right?
Yes, from the 10th to the 20th. But I’ll be back before the piano is delivered. I promise.
I trust you. You know, once you’ve delivered this project, everyone in Lyon will know your name.
For now, the only person who shouts my name at night is my daughter. And she can’t even talk yet.

The typical Romanian mistake: "Quand je finis, je t’appellerai." In French, after "quand" with a future meaning you use the FUTURE, not the present: "Quand j’aurai fini, je t’appellerai" (or "Quand je finirai…"). Romanian uses the present ("când termin"); French doesn’t. (English does the same as Romanian: "when I finish".)
3. Done by a point in the future
With d’ici, dans, avant, à + date, the future perfect shows what will already be finished at that moment:
By the end of July we’ll have finished the main structure.
I’ll be back before the piano is delivered.
In ten years, Rose-Hélène will have learned three languages.
The future perfect can express an ASSUMPTION about something that has already happened, like English "must have + participle":
Le fournisseur aura mal noté la date.
The supplier must have written down the wrong date.
Il n’est pas là ? Il aura oublié.
Elle ne répond pas, elle sera partie.
She isn’t answering, she must have left.
It’s very common in speech, to explain a delay or an absence without knowing for sure.
Je serai partie avant six heures.
Quand j’aurai fini, je t’appellerai. (I finish first)
The order: future perfect (first) → simple future (then). "Quand tu auras mangé, tu pourras sortir."

On Monday 12 June, Rose-Hélène started at the Petits Canuts nursery, two streets from the flat. Ioana had packed the bag the night before, checking the list three times: nappies, bottles, spare clothes, and the cuddly toy, a little grey rabbit given by Manon.

The first day went well. Rose-Hélène looked at the other babies with curiosity, chewed a wooden block and smiled at Madame Faure, the director. Ioana stayed an hour, as planned, then went out for ten minutes. When she came back, her daughter hadn’t even noticed.

On the third day, however, Rose-Hélène understood. The moment Ioana put on her coat, she began to scream, holding out her arms towards her mother. Madame Faure picked her up gently. "Go," she said. "As soon as you’ve closed the door, she’ll calm down. I promise."

Ioana went out. She sat down on a bench opposite the nursery and cried for twenty minutes, like a child. An old lady walking her dog stopped. "The nursery?" she asked. "I cried too. In 1975. My son is forty-nine now. He got over it. I haven’t yet."

At noon, Madame Faure sent a photo: Rose-Hélène was sleeping peacefully, the grey rabbit under her chin. Ioana showed the photo to the whole office. Nathalie said she should have started with that on the first day: we would have gained a week of work.

Meanwhile, the Fourvière site was moving forward. The parquet had finally arrived, ten days late. The supplier had sworn he had written down the right date; Ioana had found the mistake in her own email. She hadn’t said anything. A week without sleep, she had thought, can make you write 14 instead of 4.

The workers laid the parquet under the watchful eye of Monsieur Petit, who had set up his chair in the corridor to keep an eye on the works. He wrote everything down in a notebook. "When they’ve finished," he told anyone who would listen, "I’ll have written the complete history of this room."

On Saturday 24 June, Julien gave his pupils’ end-of-year concert in the Croix-Rousse community hall. Twenty-three children, aged six to fifteen, were each going to play a piece. Julien was more nervous than all of them put together.

The whole family was there: Ioana with Rose-Hélène in a baby carrier, Radu and Lucia, Odile, and even Hélène, brought by taxi by Monsieur Garnier, her nephew. The hall was full. Parents were filming on their phones, grandparents were looking for their glasses, little brothers were running between the chairs.

The concert began with a six-year-old girl who played "Au clair de la lune" with two fingers, very slowly, sticking out her tongue in concentration. She got the loudest applause of the evening. After that, the pieces became more and more difficult.

Théo played last. He had chosen a piece by Chopin, a waltz, of course. Since the concert in March, the one during which Rose-Hélène had been born, he had become a minor celebrity in the neighbourhood. He played without a score, his eyes half closed, and when he finished, the hall rose to its feet.

After the concert, while the parents were stacking the chairs, a white-haired man came up to Julien. He was wearing an elegant grey suit and holding a programme. Julien recognised him immediately and turned pale.

It was Olivier Marchand, his former piano teacher, the one who had taught him everything when he was a student. Fifteen years earlier he had left Lyon for Paris. Today he ran the teaching department of the Paris Conservatoire, one of the most prestigious music schools in the world.

"I came for you, Julien," he said simply. "People told me about your pupils. That boy, Théo, has twelve years of work in his fingers, and he’s thirteen. You did that." Julien didn’t know what to answer. He stammered a thank you.

Marchand lowered his voice. "One of our teachers is retiring in December. We’re looking for someone to train future piano teachers. Someone who knows how to talk to children. I thought of you. The post starts in January. In Paris, of course."

Julien looked over his teacher’s shoulder. At the back of the hall, Ioana was laughing with Lucia, Rose-Hélène asleep against her chest. Hélène, sitting in the front row, was talking to the six-year-old girl, who was showing her her two magic fingers.

"I’m not asking you to answer tonight," Marchand went on. "Once you’ve talked it over with your wife, call me. But I’ll need an answer by 15 July. After that, the committee will have chosen someone else." He handed him a business card and left.

Julien stood still for a long time, the card in his hand. Paris. The Conservatoire. It had been the dream of his twenties, the one he had given up when he became a teacher at a small neighbourhood school. And now that this dream was knocking at the door, he no longer knew whether he wanted it.

In the street, Radu and Lucia walked ahead, hand in hand. They had news too: as soon as Radu has finished his Erasmus year, they will move in together in a little studio under the roof, near the Place de la Croix-Rousse. "By September we’ll have repainted everything," Lucia promised. "And once we’ve bought a sofa, you’ll come for dinner."

On the way home he hardly said a word. Ioana thought he was tired. Radu told jokes; Lucia sang. Hélène, whom they had taken back to Fourvière, held his hand a little longer than usual, looking at him closely, as if she had guessed something.

That evening, once Ioana was asleep, Julien sat down at the piano without playing. The two scores were still there, side by side: Henri’s waltz, and his own, the one from the sleepless nights. Henri had left, long ago, and he had never come back.

He took Marchand’s card and placed it between the two scores. Then he thought of Ioana, of the Fourvière site, of the September inauguration, of Radu who had just decided to stay, of Hélène and her eighty-six years, of Odile who looked after the little one on Wednesdays.

"Tomorrow," he murmured. "When I’ve slept, I’ll talk to her about it." But he already knew he wouldn’t sleep. At three in the morning, Rose-Hélène woke up crying. Julien went to get her, took her in his arms and began to sing to her, very softly, Henri’s waltz.

Reading text: The letter from the nursery
The nursery director writes to new parents. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end you answer 4 questions.
Dear parents, your child will soon start at the Petits Canuts nursery. Here is how the first week, which we call "settling in", will go.
On the first day, you will stay with your child for an hour. Once they have discovered the room and the toys, you will be able to leave for a few minutes.
Each day, they will stay a little longer. As soon as they have got used to eating and sleeping here, they will be able to stay all day.
Don’t worry if your child cries in the morning. Most children cry when their parents leave, and smile five minutes later. By Friday they will have made friends.
Bring an object from home, a cuddly toy or a piece of clothing that smells of you. Once you have left, your child will keep it close and will feel safe.
And you, parents, take care of yourselves. The first separations are often harder for the adults than for the babies. Madame Faure, director.
